1:
Keil and Delitzsch sets the vision in the shape of the book. Its last part contains five visions, of which the first four open with the same formula and the fifth with a different one; the four symbolize judgments already fallen in part and in part still to fall, while the fifth proclaims the overthrow of the old order and the eventual restoration. He divides the four into two pairs, since the first two answer the prophet's intercession with a promise that Jacob shall be spared, while in the second two any further sparing is expressly refused. Gill marks the change of manner rather than matter: the ruin of the ten tribes was set out before in prophecy and is now in vision, the more to work upon the people. Henry states the lesson at once, that God bears long with a provoking people but will not bear always, and showed the prophet both what he was doing and what he designed.

What was formed is settled from husbandry. Clarke and Ellicott agree the creatures are locusts, not grasshoppers. Clarke explains the timing: the early crop had been mowed and housed and the second not yet begun, so that by the king's mowings we may understand the first crop, a portion of which the king probably claimed as the better hay, though the words may mean simply the prime crop; one writer, he adds, took it of the shearing of the king's sheep. Ellicott hears a complaint, that the king claimed tyrannically the first-fruits of the hay. Wesley explains why the second growth mattered, since the first shooting was often too luxuriant and was eaten down with cattle, so that if the second were destroyed the whole harvest was marred. Henry adds that God formed these creatures not only as his creatures but as instruments of his wrath, and remarks how much of the wisdom and power of God appears in minute animals, as much in the structure of an ant as of an elephant. Calvin sets aside as forced two renderings which make the first word a noun, creation or a swarm, and keeps the plain sense that the Lord formed locusts in the prophet's presence.

What the locusts stand for is where the readings diverge. Gill takes them for an invasion of the northern kingdom rather than of Judea. Clarke reads them as symbols of the enemies that had impoverished the land, and quotes a remark that after the death of the second Jeroboam the kingdom was so weakened that it had to have recourse to strangers, the application made to Pul beginning the final misery of the state. Calvin fixes the vision earlier still, comparing the time before that king's reign with the prosperity that followed, the kingdom having then been laid waste by hostile incursions, drought, inclement weather and pestilence. He takes locusts for a moderate punishment, standing metaphorically for invasions which desolated the country without laying the whole waste; and he draws the moral, that though the people saw their land consumed they did not think God displeased with them, since ungodly men will not examine themselves nor lift their eyes to heaven when chastised, but grow stupid in their calamities.

Ellicott holds the received rendering of the plea incorrect, and would have it run, who is Jacob that he should stand, for he is small. Gill has the Lord hearing the prayer and averting the judgment at the prophet's intercession, so that the fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much. On the repenting all agree that the language is human, Wesley saying so in five words and Ellicott comparing other places where the same is said of God; Gill puts the distinction most carefully, that as men when they repent desist from what they were doing, so the Lord desisted, not changing his mind but changing the dispensations of his providence.
4:
That the second judgment is heavier than the first is agreed, and Calvin makes it a rule. Locusts stand for a moderate punishment, and though the famine they bring is a grievous evil, fire strikes men with much greater dread; so the figure shows that God had become very indignant, having found the people hardened and past reforming by common remedies. This, Calvin says, is God's usual way of proceeding: at first he tries whether men are capable of being healed and applies not the most grievous punishment but such as may be endured, and when he perceives hardness and obstinacy he doubles and trebles it, and at last increases his judgments sevenfold. He adds a grammatical remark, that the pointing of the word here settles the form of the corresponding word in the first vision and shows those mistaken who rendered it creation.

What the fire itself represents is read historically by one and poetically by another. Clarke takes it for war, both civil and foreign, permitted to harass the land after the death of the second Jeroboam, wars which would have destroyed it entirely had the prophet not interceded; all this, he says, God caused to pass before the eyes of Amos in the vision of prophecy, intimating that at the intercession of his prophets total ruin should be prevented. Ellicott keeps to the picture: this is the description of a yet more terrible calamity, the word rendered contend meaning to punish by fire, and the image being that of a prairie fire eating up the later grass which the locusts had spared. He would read the portion rather than a portion, and treats the consuming of the great deep as a strong hyperbole, denying that it can well refer to the heathen world as another interpreter maintains; the sense is rather that not only the last remnant of pasture but the deepest springs of moisture are scorched up in the blaze. Wesley reads the calling as a command for fire from heaven, and the part consumed as a part of the land.

The prayer that stops it is the same as before, and so is the answer. Gill notes that the prophet uses the same argument he had used at the first vision, asking only that the calamity proceed no further, and that the Lord heard him and desisted. Calvin explains why the repetition matters. Ungodly men counted the prophets liars whenever God did not immediately execute the vengeance he had denounced; but Amos reminds them that when God defers punishment he does not threaten in vain, and waits for men to repent, so that if they go on abusing his patience they will feel at last how dreadful is the vengeance that awaits those who pervert the goodness of God and will not hear him inviting them so kindly to himself.
7:
Calvin takes this third vision as the key to the two before it. What the people had gained by their obstinacy was only to render God implacable and to make him spare them no longer, and he puts the sense into direct speech: God has borne with you hitherto according to his own goodness, but promise not yourselves that he will always deal so, for your contumacy has provoked him; there is now no forgiveness provided, and as you are incurable, so the Lord will remain unchangeable in the rigour of his judgment. On the plumbline itself he declines to be ingenious. Interpreters explain the vision in various ways and philosophize refinedly on the word, he says, and yet almost all their refinements are frigid; were he disposed to handle the passage plausibly he would make the plumbline the law of God, which prescribed a regular order that might serve as a rule; but he is not disposed to refine in that manner, and doubts not that God meant simply that this would be the last measuring.

The others read the image from the trade. Clarke takes it as an emblem of strict justice, intimating that God would now visit them according to their iniquities, and glosses the setting of the line as visiting them by justice without any mixture of mercy. Ellicott gets more out of the picture than anyone. The wall made by a plumbline is a perpendicular one, and the stability of the kingdom is represented by the closely fitting, well-jointed stones of a lofty wall; then, right in the heart of this strong-built city, the Lord himself marks out the extent of the desolation, since a plumb-line is used in dismantling buildings as well as in raising them. Wesley notices only that the wall is strongly and beautifully built.

The prophet's silence at this vision is itself remarked. Gill points out that he made no supplication here as he had done at the two former visions, and thinks the question was put to him for that reason, and because this vision carried something of moment which God would have him attend to. Calvin explains the silence by astonishment. When locusts were formed and when there was a contending by fire, the prophet might easily have gathered what God meant, since those visions were by no means ambiguous; but a Lord standing on a wall with a plumb-line was harder, and Calvin thinks God made him feel amazement on purpose, so that the people might be the more attentive, since we apply our thoughts to hidden things and attend coldly to what we suppose easily understood, while difficulty sharpens the mind. Ellicott draws the conclusion the vision forces: the passing by means sparing, and there will come a time when prayer is of no avail and all intercessions, however passionate, are too late, the door of mercy being shut.

The two things named for destruction are traced to their history. Gill takes the high places of Isaac for those the ten tribes built at Beersheba in imitation of Isaac and pleading his example, since he worshipped there, though the true God and not idols as they did; and he notes that the Greek version turns the phrase into high places of laughter, ridiculous in the eyes of the Lord. Clarke fixes the same site, where Isaac had built an altar, and observes that the place, having been abused to idolatrous uses, was afterwards demolished by Josiah. On the house of Jeroboam he supplies the whole reckoning: the Lord had promised Jehu that his family should sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation, and Zechariah the son of Jeroboam was the fourth in order after Jehu, so that the threatening fell on him, murdered by Shallum after a reign of six months, and in him the family became extinct.
10:
Gill notes that the Targum calls Amaziah the prince or president of Bethel, the word covering both offices, and thinks he had charge of civil as well as religious affairs there. Ellicott calls the passage a brief historical interlude of much interest, since it shows that the preaching had been felt both in the sanctuary at Bethel and in the palaces at Samaria, and that the chief priest, with the characteristic exaggeration of fear and anger, accuses him of treason. Gill has him fearing that Amos would alienate the people from the worship he presided over, lessening both his esteem and his worldly gain, and noticing that this time the prophet had offered no intercession. Henry puts it more sharply: the complaint was not merely that Amos prophesied without license but that he prophesied against the altars, which would soon be deserted if his preaching gained credit, as the shrine-makers of Ephesus hated the apostle whose preaching spoiled their trade; great pretenders to sanctity, he adds, are commonly the worst enemies of those really sanctified.

That the report was false is agreed. Clarke says flatly that there is not one word of truth in the message: Amos had not conspired, had not said that Jeroboam should die by the sword, and had not said that Israel should be carried away, though that last was implied in the threatening and delivered by the prophet afterwards. Gill and Wesley make the same distinction, that the sword was threatened against the house and not the person, and Gill adds that it was the king's son who in fact died so. Henry turns it round: it is the praise of great saints that they pray for their enemies, and the shame of great sinners that they are enemies to those who pray for them.

The king's silence is noticed by three voices and explained differently. Keil and Delitzsch thinks he began no proceedings because he did not regard the affair as dangerous, so the priest tried persuasion instead. Calvin offers three possibilities: that the king was not much excited, that he dared not openly take the prophet's life since Amos had gained authority among the people, or that the business was arranged between the two enemies of sound doctrine. He is clear about what the priest wanted, since conspiracy is a crime worthy of death; Amaziah expected more than he got, and when it failed his vulpine wiliness appeared, and he sent for the prophet himself.

Calvin dissects the advice that follows. He calls it the device by which Satan attempted to depress the prophet's mind, and reads the two clauses as two engines: go reminds Amos that he is at liberty and the way is open; flee tells him that unless he provides for his life it is all over with him. So an easy escape and the fear of danger were pressed on him together. Behind both, Calvin says, lay the priest's real object, to keep possession of his own place, which he could not do while the prophet stayed, since he could not contend with him in arguments; and whatever characters he had assumed, the ape now appears as the ape. Clarke reads the kindness the same way, offered by the very man who had just accused him of high treason, and observes that hireling priests have ever been the great enemies of the true prophets, accusing them of conspiracy when no charge of false doctrine would lie. Keil and Delitzsch renders the offer as an invitation to earn his bread by prophesying in Judah unhindered, and explains the prohibition from the standing of the place, a sanctuary founded by the king and a royal capital. Clarke states the principle plainly, that Amos must not speak against idolatry because idolatry was the king's religion, and one who speaks against the king's religion must be an enemy to the state.
14:
The disclaimer that heads the answer is read as a claim, not a denial. Calvin explains why: Amos denies being a prophet or a prophet's son not to make himself contemptible but to gain authority, since an extraordinary call gave him greater weight than a childhood in the schools of the prophets would have done. He was led to the office as it were by force, so that he could not lay it aside without shaking off a yoke God had laid on him. Keil and Delitzsch reads the words as repudiating a particular insinuation, that prophesying was the trade by which he got his living: no prophet by profession and no prophet's son, no pupil of the prophets' schools, but by his proper calling a herdsman of oxen and a man who plucks mulberry-figs and lives on them. Clarke has him answering the order to leave: an extraordinary messenger called for this occasion only, with no message to Judah and therefore no reason to go there, but a message to Israel which he must faithfully deliver. Ellicott calls it an interesting biographical touch, since prophecy, like other occupations, tended to form a hereditary guild, and Amos was not by birth of it. Wesley says it in three phrases, not originally, nor by study, nor by any human designation.

The second occupation draws a note on ancient husbandry. Ellicott reports that the Greek and Latin versions render the word for gatherer as nipper or pincher, and that two ancient naturalists describe a custom of pinching the mulberry-fig to make it ripen; but he thinks it very doubtful whether this is the sense of the Hebrew word, which is nowhere else employed. Gill turns from the trade to the calling: Amos did not seek the office nor take the honour to himself, which shows his mission divine and free of lucrative views, as God took David from the same state of life and Elisha from the plough. Ellicott adds that nothing here hints at a lack of education or refinement, the inward call having been more than sufficient.

The retort is noticed for its exact form. Keil and Delitzsch observes that Amos meets the words thou shalt not prophesy with the keen counter, thus saith Jehovah, and traces the verb rendered drop to the Song of Moses, where the teaching drips as the rain. Calvin makes the opposition the point: who art thou, he has the prophet say, thou speakest thus, but God will speak in his turn; and he marks the difference between the two speeches, since the impostor's attempt to frighten a holy man was vain while God's word would not be without effect, so that whether the prophet held his peace or spoke, the vengeance hung over the priest.

The sentence is read as punishing the interference, not only the idolatry. Calvin presses the connecting word: Amaziah suffered not merely for corrupting God's worship and making gain by the disguise of religion, but because he had dared to oppose the authority of God and turn the prophet from his office, by hidden craft and open violence alike; destruction is doubly increased, he says, when men set an iron neck against a God who would have them pliant and asks only that they confess they have sinned. Clarke sets out the four parts of the doom and grants that since we hear no more of this priest we cannot tell how the threatenings were executed; he notes too that the last clause declares openly what Amos had not said before, though it had been made the substance of the accusation against him. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on the harshest clause, that the wife is made a harlot by violation at the taking of the city; Ellicott identifies the polluted land as the land of exile, since food eaten anywhere but in Canaan was reckoned unclean.
